@@61897155 <p> The Bookseller - Wales Focushttps : **34;971;TOOLONG ... enJane Davidson ' I think some of the best and most exciting ideas come out of small countries'https : **29;1007;TOOLONG ... &lt;div class= " field field-name-field-image field-type-image field-label-hidden " &gt;&lt;div class= " field-items " &gt;&lt;div class= " field-item even " &gt;&lt;img typeof= " foaf:Image " src= " https : **34;1038;TOOLONG ... width= " 192 " height= " 181 " alt= " " **45;1074;TOOLONG ... class= " field field-name-body **28;1121;TOOLONG field-label-hidden " &gt;&lt;div class= " field-items " &gt;&lt;div class= " field-item even " property= " content:encoded " &gt;&lt;p&gt;I live in the most incredibly beautiful , warm , bilingual -- therefore culturally different -- and special place . And I want people to know more about it . " So says Jane Davidson , formerly minister for environment , sustainability and housing in the Welsh government , and now the author of &lt;em&gt;#futuregen : Lessons from a Small Country&lt;/em&gt; . It 's a book that does indeed focus attention on her adopted home nation of Wales , and it also provides considerable food for thought for those interested in how we might tackle the momentous issues that face us , both locally and globally . As Nikhil Seth , UN assistant secretary-general , has said : " What Wales is doing today , the world will do tomorrow " . &lt;/p&gt; **40;1151;TOOLONG charts the pivotal role Davidson and others played in the genesis of the Well-being of Future Generations ( Wales ) Act 2015 , the first piece of legislation in history to place regenerative and sustainable practice at the heart of government . It creates seven goals for living within Wales ' environmental limits in the arenas of health , prosperity , resilience , communities , language and heritage , equality and Wales ' role in the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;While the main focus of the book is the genesis of the act 's creation , a story told with the help of numerous other contributors , Davidson injects an elementof memoir too , emphasising&amp;nbsp ; the importance of personal experience as a driver for action . Now in her 60s , she was brought up in Africa . " Both my parents were doctors , and passionate about good health , particularly in a developing country like Zimbabwe , or Rhodesia as it was then . My father was a public health doctor , my mother latterly became a GP and did a lot of family planning support when she was in Africa . " &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; " All the way through , there was this attitude that work was about service to others . As a child I also spent a lot of time exploring outdoors on my cycle rides , and had the feeling of being part of this big nature tableau . " When Davidson was later sent to a British boarding school in the 1970s , it came as an " utter shock " , she says . Once there , she learned a lesson about sustainability , finding her fellow students ' devotion to first-world frivolities like fashion hard to understand . A lifelong dislike of waste was the result . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The legacy of her formative years led Davidson to institute the first plastic bag charge in the UK ; a Climate Change Commission for Wales , and waste legislation that transformed Wales ' record on recycling . " Wales is now up there fighting with Germany to be best in the world , which is incredibly exciting , " she tells me . Davidson was also instrumental in the creation of the Llwybr Arfordir Cymru ; the Wales Coast Path , which now runs the entire 870-mile length of the Welsh coastline ; and she herself now lives close to the path , on a small-holding in Pembrokeshire , where she and her family try to live as sustainably as possible . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;I ask Davidson if being a small country , as her subtitle suggests , is what has made Wales nimble in its aspirations for change . " Yes , like the carrier bag charge , I think some of the best and most exciting ideas come out of small countries because often they 're the right size in which to test them . Wales also has a very small population , and so a lot of its land is green and very beautiful . People do really appreciate the nature around them , and that 's why the creation of the Wales Coast Path absolutely drove me , because it was another way that people could connect with the shape of their nation . " &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Described by Davidson as " a beacon of hope in a time of despair " , the Well-being of Future Generations Act is impressive not only for its content but for its long- term vision . In **31;1193;TOOLONG , she was keen to reflect on what government is for . " I believe its job is to try and ensure that at the end of its administration , life is better for all people , " she says . " But what I have so often seen over the years is that life is better for those who have money , but not for those who neither have the vote nor influence ... notably our young people . I think that a fundamental proposition of government is to secure everybody 's future : inter- generational justice and fairness is really important . " &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;When it comes to implementing lessons leaned from the Covid-19 crisis , Wales might be a good place to look . In the light of the pandemic , Davidson , now pro vice-chancellor emeritus at the University of Wales Trinity Saint David , has added a new postscript to her book . " When this threat is over , " she writes , " there will be an opportunity to capitalise on our rediscovered kindness and sense of society , to celebrate the importance of nature , to build on our increased virtual engagement to act on that other silent killer -- climate change -- for the benefit of current and future generations . We know now that governments can act -- and quickly -- when faced with an emergency ... #futuregen is one path open to them . However , in September Williams was appointed to the post , and since then she has been on a whirlwind tour of Welsh schools -- until the lockdown , that is. &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The two-year post was introduced to raise the visibility of children 's literature in Wales , help develop children 's literacy skills and support the next generation of writers . It followed the release of Literature Wales ' Strategic Plan for 2019 -- 22 , which outlined children and young people as one of its main priorities , with a particular focus on engag- ing those from BAME and low-income backgrounds , as well as those with disabilities or illnesses . Williams says that in addition to promoting the importance of children 's literature , her aim is to " engage with as many kids as I can " . The connection is really helping them to see that they can be a writer in the future , if they want to be . " &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Williams became a published author herself five years ago , following a decade of working as an actor . She was shortlisted for her entry , which became her first novel with the Welsh kids ' publisher , &lt;em&gt;Elen 's Island&lt;/em&gt; . Though she had not previously intended to write for children , it " made sense " once she began to , building on her experience working with chil- dren through drama workshops in her previous career . It 's fun , and you get honest feedback from them . Other early titles included Wales-focused tourism books and a wildlife series . More Gaspard books in print and digital are coming later in the year and in 2021 , with the next instalment , Gaspard 's Foxtrot , scheduled for release in June . The story is also being adapted into a new orchestral tale for children , composed by Jonathan Dove ; it will be performed by the Philharmonia Orchestra across the UK in 2021 -- 22. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Another exciting new development for the publisher this year is the launch of new photographic book imprint Bird 's Eye Books . The list is kicking off this autumn with &lt;em&gt;Bird'sEye London&lt;/em&gt; by aerial photographer Paul Campbell , &lt;br&gt; a collection of pictures taken by Campbell from a helicopter ; the indie promises it will unearth new perspectives of the city and its landmarks . It will be published in e-book and hardback format on 15th October 2020 , with an r.r.p. of ? 35 . Other Bird 's Eye Books titles to follow in 2021 include a book about Atlantic puffins , a photographic portrait of the changing lives of nomadic tribes in central Asia , and a title focusing on peonies by nurseryman and horticulturist Alec White , which will have a special limited edition launched at next year 's Chelsea Flower Show . Graffeg has also just signed photographer Charles Hawes ' &lt;em&gt;Welsh Gardens from Above&lt;/em&gt; , the first in a new series of garden books featuring Hawes ' photographs taken with a drone camera . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Next week , Graffeg will publish &lt;em&gt;Behind the Mask &lt;/em&gt;by photographer Glenn Dene and Dr Ami Jones , about Nevill Hall Hospital in Abergavenny 's NHS staff and their attempts to deal with Covid-19 ( publishing on 4th June ) . The indie has responded to the pandemic in other ways , too . Last month , it launched the &lt;em&gt;Help Your Neighbour&lt;/em&gt; campaign , offering its customers the opportunity to purchase books for others at a 50% discount , and this month it introduced the Help your Bookshop initiative , which sees the publisher return a 25% trade commission to indie bookshops for customer orders placed on its website. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Looking ahead , Graffeg is planning to move its sales and distribution base in Carmarthenshire to a retail outlet in the area that has space for a bookshop , and the space to host events . It hopes to do so within the next 12 to 24 months . Gill says of the move : " We have been considering a high street presence for some time , as a destination for authors , retailers and customers to meet us , join our author events , and view , browse and buy our complete range of titles . " For now though , Gill says that Graffeg 's focus is " survival " , but with so many exciting developments on the cards , it looks set to bounce back from the lockdown in good health . &lt;/p&gt; **36;3953;TOOLONG &lt;span class= " date-display-single " property= " dc:date " datatype= " xsd:dateTime " content= " **25;3991;TOOLONG " &gt;May 28 , 2020&lt;/span&gt;&lt;div class= " field **27;4018;TOOLONG field-type-text field-label-above " &gt;&lt;div class= " field-label " &gt;Written By : &amp;nbsp ; Residing in the Culture , Sport and Tourism portfolio , we are an agency of the Welsh Government responsible for promoting our creative sector in Wales and internationally . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Creative Wales will champion the creative industries in Wales , providing a strong , unified voice for the sector . Our mission is to drive growth across the creative industries , buildon existing success and develop&amp;nbsp ; new talentand skills , positioning Wales as one of the best places for creative businesses to thrive . We will promote Wales to the world , connecting and showcasing our best creative minds and businesses . We&amp;nbsp ; will drive growth across the whole of the nation through targeted regional activity . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Our initial focus will be on three sub-sectors : film and TV ; digital and gaming ; and music . We will also focus on the publishing industry , through our support to the Books Council of Wales ( BCW ) . &lt;/p&gt; **26;6354;TOOLONG was Creative Wales set up ? **25;6382;TOOLONG The time was right to support growth from a grass-roots level , as well as continuing to invest in our already successful high-end television , film , digital media and publishing sectors . Our primary measures of success will be economic , such as increased turnover , numbers of workers , business births , retained IP and spend in the Welsh economy . Broader benefits are expected to include a stronger supply chain , improved skills , cultural and social benefits . &lt;/p&gt; **26;6409;TOOLONG will you support and engage with the publishing industry ? **25;6437;TOOLONG A healthy publishing industry is an essential part of Wales ' cultural identity . It supports other creative industries through the content it produces , and provides an income and opportunities to those employed in the industry . At the Creative Wales launch , we highlighted the importance of publishing to the creative indus- tries and identified it as a key sector for growth . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Our funding and support for the publishing industry is channelled through BCW . Working closely with BCW , our aim is to support a successful , bilingual publishing industry that not only makes a contribution to our wider economic growth strategy for the creative industries in Wales , but also supports our wider objectives , including support for rural communities and local economies , and our commitment to delivering Welsh Government 's Welsh Language Strategy and reaching the goal of a million Welsh speakers by 2050. &lt;/p&gt; **26;6464;TOOLONG has your work been impacted by the coronavirus pandemic ? **25;6492;TOOLONG We have been in close contact with BCW from a very early stage , to identify the impact on the publishing sector in Wales and how we can best provide support . On 1st April , we announced additional funding for BCW to help respond to the needs of the publishing industry in the face of the Covid-19 crisis . A proportion of this funding has been distributed to independent high-street bookshops in Wales , to ensure they can sustain their business over the coming months . In addition , there is an emergency fund for publishers of both books and magazines who have their head office in Wales . &lt;/p&gt; **27;6519;TOOLONG are Creative Wales ' future plans ? **25;6548;TOOLONG Establishing Creative Wales as a discrete function within Welsh Government enables us to be more responsive and flexible to the needs of such a diverse sector . We want to : grow the sector in Wales ; develop the right skills ; raise standards and promote diversity and equality across the sector ; simplify our funding support for the creative sector , responding at a fast pace ; and build our new Creative Wales brand to market and promote the creative sector in Wales to the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;We will also be recruiting an advisory board of industry experts to support the Creative Wales team by helping to gather ideas and insights from the creative industries in Wales and internationally , and identifying new oppor- tunities for future growth across the sector . &lt;/p&gt; @@61897332 <h> Seamus Enright <p> Published : May 31 , 2020 , 03:00 <p> Tenders for ? 4.4m flood defence scheme due <h> Tenders for ? 4.4m flood defence scheme due <h> ? 410k cost to fix damage following recent flooding <p> Tenderdocuments are " currently being prepared " seeking a range of consultancy services to oversee the design and implementation of a multi-million euro flood relief scheme for Cavan Town and its environs . <p> The Anglo-Celt understands that Cavan County Council is in the final stages of preparing the necessary documents , the latest stage in progressing design of the new ? 4.44 million Cavan Town Flood Relief Scheme . <p> Approved under the Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management ( CFRAM ) , the scheme is being progressed by the local authority in partnership with the Office of Public Works ( OPW ) . <p> It 's hoped a consultant can be in place by September 2020 . <p> It follows the inclusion of Cavan Town in a ? 257 million investment across 50 flood relief projects nationwide , announced in May 2019 . <p> The latest development comes as the council is counting the cost of recent flooding events , which ravaged many parts of the county . <p> It was impossible for the local authority to put an accurate estimate on the cost of the damage until waters receded full , at which stage a full assessment of any repairs needed on the road network and any associated costs was carried out . <p> Along with having to fork out an estimated ? 10,000 for clean up and repairs arising out of the flooding caused by three storms - Ciara , Dennis and Jorge - all within a month , drainage repairs and remedial works at 18 countywide locations are set to cost the authority approximately ? 100,000 . <p> A spokesperson further confirmed : " Cavan County Council is currently seeking additional funding in excess of ? 300,000 for necessary remedial works at 25 locations . Priority locations for additional funding applications are where homes have been flooded or where residents have been cut off by flood waters . " <p> In the Council 's recently approved Budget 2020 , members approved allocating just shy of ? 210,000 to tackle ' Climate Change and Flooding ' , which will go towards improving land and road drainage as outlined in the local authority 's own ' Climate Change Strategy ' . <p> The new allocation also coincides with the redrafting of responsibilities of Strategic Policy Committees within the local authority , which saw the former ' Environment and Planning ' SPC become ' Climate and Biodiversity Action , and Environment ' . <p> The Council is still assisting four families in Cavan applying for the once-off voluntary relocation scheme for homeowners worst affected by flooding in the county three years ago . <p> Over 80 roads were flooded , 20 homes damaged and 113 more cut-off by flooding over that almost three month period , with the Council estimating the cost by damage incurred in excess of ? 3.5 million . <p> A sum of ? 205,000 previously received by the Council was used to provide a scheme of earth embankment , culvert and flood wall defences to tackle persistent flooding in the Drumullan area outside Cavan Town . The funding also covered drainage measures and actions aimed at addressing factors that otherwise left these homes vulnerable in the past . 
@@61897548 <h> How Important is Art as a Form of Protest ? <p> Given the current political climate , we here at frieze have been reflecting on the role of art in responding to conflict . With this in mind , we invited a cross-section of artists , curators and writers to answer two deceptively simple questions : ' How important is art as a form of protest ? ' and ' How effective is it as a conduit of change ? ' Responses could take the form of a statement , an image , a film or a combination of all three . The submissions , by more than 50 respondents from over 30 countries are provocative and enlightening . Further contributions to the print version are included here , from around the world . ( Click on the artist 's name below to jump to their entry . ) <p> Vernon Ah KeeVernon Ah Kee lives in Brisbane , Australia . Earlier this year , he had a solo show , ' Not an Animal or a Plant ' , at the NAS Gallery , Sydney . He is participating in the inaugural Honolulu Biennial , which runs until 8 May . <p> Jonathas de AndradeJonathas de Andrade lives in Recife , Brazil . His video The Uprising will be on display at the Museum of Modern Art , New York , as part of ' Unfinished Conversations : New Work from the Collection ' which runs until 30 July . His solo show , ' O Peixe ' , at the New Museum , New York , runs until 9 April . His work is included in the Sharjah Biennial until 12 June . <p> Daniel G. And ? jarDaniel G. And ? jar lives in Barcelona , Spain . His work is included in documenta 14 . <p> Art must be a sign of resistance to a political model that is increasingly hierarchical , diffuse , global and standardized . The public stage has become a sort of orchestrated video game -- a frivolous , ridiculous operetta with a few recited parts that are performed daily before a people overwhelmed by the consequences of the crisis . The audience is immediately proscribed by the mass media and , therefore , defused before its fellow citizens dare ' boo ' from the stands . This is the criminalization of protest , which leads to the brutalization of audiences implemented by refined political techniques -- in short , to audiences that dare practise disobedience to the rules imposed by the institution , such as transgression , insubordination , the creation of new political experiences or the rehearsal of new voices . Democracy has become an aesthetic matter . I want to get away from unilateral , closed discourses affording no possibility for response , participation or interaction . We artists have a political function that requires clear ethical positions . Language can change the world -- or should . This is one of the artist 's most effective tools . <p> Andreas AngelidakisAndreas Angelidakis lives in Athens , Greece . His work is included in documenta 14 . In November , he is curating Regionale 17 at Kunsthalle Basel . Until the end of the year , he will continue to work on Kalejdohill , an experiment in citizen participation in Stockholm . <p> For the last five years , I 've been working with the legendary transgender activist Paola Revenioti . Originally , my aim was to make her work known to a broader audience outside of Greece , so we began in 2013 with an interview in Candy magazine and then organized a show of her photographs at Breeder Gallery . Her work is pure protest ; her magazine Kraximo ( Gay Bashing ) was the only outlet for reports of police brutality against LGBT+ citizens in the 1980s . There is a transcendent quality to her work , even if it 's just a Facebook post , a YouTube video or an archival photograph . I do n't know if showing her work in an art context would qualify as protest , but it certainly shed light on the history and current state of the fight for trans visibility and human rights . Last month , Revenioti 's documentary about Dimitra , a trans woman living on the island of Lesvos , was broadcast on national television : that 's a long way to go for someone whom society only expected to prostitute for a living . Change takes time , but every effort is worth it . <p> Paola Revenioti , photograph , 1985 . Courtesy : Private collection <p> Leonor AntunesLeonor Antunes lives in Berlin , Germany . Earlier this year , she had a solo show at Air de Paris , Paris . This year , her work will be included in the 57th Venice Biennale . <p> Two weeks after the election of Donald Trump , I held a small event in Amsterdam in a place called the Hubertus House , which was designed by the architect Aldo van Eyck in 1959 . I called it An Open House . I have been working on this project for quite a long time ; I was invited to do it by the curating collective If I Ca n't Dance I Do n't Want to Be Part of Your Revolution . Van Eyck designed two interconnected buildings to host single mothers and their children in a private foundation that provided day care , as well as other support . Initially , I did n't plan to work on this project in the way that I did but after the shock of the election , I could n't think of anything else apart from reacting somehow . <p> The project included 12 women , myself included , from different backgrounds and origins -- we all look very different from each other . Tess van Eyck , the architect 's daughter , joined us , sitting on a sofa reading her newspaper . For one hour , we all stood on the balconies of the building and behind the windows . The public was told nothing about what they might see ; they were allowed access to one of the two buildings , but not the one we were occupying . We were all dressed in the 12 different colours that Van Eyck used . <p> Kader AttiaKader Attia lives in Berlin , Germany . His solo show at theMuseum of Contemporary Art Australia , Sydney , runs from12 April to 30 July ; his solo show at S.M.A.K , Ghent , Belgium , runs until 1 October . This year , his work will also be included in exhibitions at Lehmann Maupin , New York , Mary and Leigh Block Museum of Art , Northwestern University , Evanston , and Galleria Continua , San Gimignano . <p> Walead BeshtyWalead Beshty lives in Los Angeles , USA . His solo show at Petzel , New York , USA , runs from 20 April to 17 June ; his solo show at Rat Hole Gallery , Tokyo , runs until 29 April . ' Picture Industry ' , a provisional history of the technological image ( 1860 to the present ) , curated by Beshty , will be on view at the Hessel Museum of Art , Center for Curatorial Studies , Bard College , from 23 June to 10 September . <p> Art is a discourse about aesthetics staged through aesthetics . ( I use that word in the original Greek sense , referring to perceptible things , the study of which concernsthe means by which something becomes knowable to the senses . ) Art 's political potential derives from expanding the conditions of aesthetics , of what can be perceived , and distributing this perception in new configurations while being grounded in a set of parameters , i.e. its history , its venues and its conventions . In this sense , art modifies what is held in common , and it does this by tweaking and thereby challenging aesthetic conventions a few at a time ; its movement is an improvisation within tradition , and its effect is gradual . <p> Art 's most potent political impact is achieved by its ability to intervene within conventions that are intertwined with histories of dominance and subordination , inclusion and exclusion , denaturalizing them and , by extension , democratizing experience . But , to exist , art requires infrastructure -- to call something art is to assume a massive system of institutions and professionals , buildings and bureaucracies , histories and discourses . For this reason , art can rarely , if ever , intervene in civic life on its own terms . Instead , it acts within the systems it is inextricable from -- and these systems are slow to evolve . Protest , on the other hand , is an expression of institutional crisis . It is a civic act in both production and execution . Protest is quick , fluid , forceful and , by definition , it eschews the solidity of institutions . Protest appears when the social contract has been violated in some way ; it defies the institution 's authority to decide who has permission to speak and who does not , and the form that speech can take . Protest arises when institutions can no longer adequately contain the flow of the polis . It is a rupture and is evidence of a failure of institutions , thus it acts outside of and in opposition to institutional strictures . Protest circumvents the orderly arrangements of institutions ; it does not negotiate with institutional parameters as art does ; it does not tweak its rules , it refuses them on the basis of their corruption . Protest is a means to become a public , a citizenry , outside of the avenues prescribed by institutions . <p> In the face of crisis , art often reverts to the false promise of institutional inclusion , for it claims , albeit tacitly , that the institutional voice can speak for the excluded : the very failure that gives rise to protest . In the moments that necessitate protest , the voice of art is insufficient at best and oppositional at worst : for , the institutional system through which it speaks is the very thing that protest questions . When art masquerades as protest , it undermines its own capacities to expand perception ; but , more troublingly , it nullifies protest by creating a false representation of it , institutionalizing that which is opposed to the institution itself . The former is relatively harmless -- it just results in mediocre art -- but the latter is insidious , since it forecloses the pathways that only protest can open up , offering a placebo where real action is required . <p> David BirkinDavid Birkin lives in New York , USA . @@61898626 <h> Snow Mass Estimates and The Future of Ski Resorts <p> Climate projections of natural snow conditions are regularly viewed as alarming for the future of ski resorts . By 2050 , Arctic summers may be ice-free , the ski season might be cut short by half , and Siberia could become habitable . <p> A report from the European Space Agency 's Climate Change Initiative has unveiled the first reliable estimate of snow mass change . This has helped to identify different continental trends . And new data analysis predicts that the Arctic Ocean could become ice-free by 2050 . <p> Human influence on the climate system is evident . Greenhouse gases are the highest they have ever been in history . The implications and consequences of the results can potentially transform life on the planet as we know it . Skiing might even become a vintage sport . All in all , it seems like trying to reduce climate change has never been so urgent . <h> Snow mass estimates are now more reliable , for the first time <p> A report from the European Space Agency 's Climate Change Initiative has unveiled the first reliable estimate of snow mass change . This has helped to identify different continental trends . <p> As part of ESA 's Climate Change Initiative , researchers from the Finnish Meteorological Institute ( FMI ) and the Environment and Climate Change Canada have reliably estimated the amount of annual snow mass and changes in snow cover in the Northern Hemisphere between 1980 and 2018 . <p> The study was the result of a 39-year snow mass climate data record which was based on passive microwave satellite observations combined with ground-based snow depth measurements . <p> The research team led by Professor Jouni Pulliainen , the paper 's lead author , Research Professor at FMI , and Director at the Arctic Research and Arctic Space Centre of the Finnish Meteorological Institute found little reduction in Northern Hemisphere snow mass over the course of the four decades of satellite observations when looking at the annual maximum amount of snow at the turn of February-March . More reliable estimates identified different continental trends , with snow mass decreased by 46 gigatonnes per decade across North America . <p> According to Jouni Pulliainen , in the past , " estimates of global and regional snowfall trends have only been indicative . " And " the results show that the amount of rainfall has increased in the northern regions , especially in the northern parts of Asia . " <p> ESA 's Climate Change Initiative is a research and development program that merges and calibrates measurements from multiple satellite missions to generate a global time-series . <h> Snow as a water source : Why snow mass data is important <p> The amount of seasonal snow is paramount for the survival of ski resorts around the world . Estimating the amount of seasonal snow is also important for understanding the water cycle and Earth 's climate system . Snow is fundamental for the survival of several animals , too . Millions of people rely on snow meltwaters for power , irrigation , and even drinking water . <p> Warming surface temperatures due to climate change have driven substantial reductions in the snow cover in both its extent and its duration . Snow mass --the amount of water held in the snow pack--has changed over time . However , establishing a clear and coherent picture of its change has proven difficult . <p> Having more accurate snow mass information will not only help to assess the availability of freshwater resources and identify flood risk , but will also enable better assessment of the role seasonal snow plays in the climate system . <p> Snow could also become a source of electricty , if only there were enough snow in the future . In 2019 , UCLA researchers engineered a new device that can generate electricity from falling snow called a snow-based triboelectric nanogenerator , or snow TENG . <h> How snow conditions and climate observations affect ski resorts <p> Ski tourism is a major sector of a mountain region 's economy , which is under the threat of long-term climate change . <p> According to Snow Forecast , a source of snow-related news and useful information for ski resorts and ski enthusiasts , Japan is the country that has the most ski resorts : 543 , followed by The United States with 447 , and Austria with 317 . <p> There are 228 ski resorts in Italy , and Switzerland has 211 from a total of 3,200 ski resorts around the world . Climate projections of natural snow conditions are regularly viewed as alarming for the future of ski resorts . <p> Since Ruka in Lapland , one of Finland 's largest and more modern ski resorts started to close in early May rather than in early June , the ski area with the longest ski season in the world is now Arapahoe Basin in Colorado in The United States . <p> The ski season is getting cut short every year due to global warming . According to the National Snow and Ice Data Center ( NSIDC ) , if the climate continues to change at the current rate , warmer winters will mean even shorter ski seasons , with the average ski season length being cut by half by 2050 . <p> Global warming could change the planet so dramatically that it could make large parts of Siberia suitable for sustaining human populations . <h> Ice-free Arctic summers by 2050 <p> Ice-free Arctic in the winter months appears possible if carbon dioxide continues to be emitted at high levels /Source : Climate Change Initiave , ESA <p> Analysis by ESA 's Climate Change Initiative using global climate models predicts that most of the Arctic Ocean could become ice-free during summer by 2050 . The observations suggest that the future of the Arctic 's sea-ice cover critically depends on future carbon dioxide emissions . <p> Data analysis of satellite-based measurements from the 1970s shows a trend of more ice melting away during summers and less new ice forming during winters . In September 2019 , the daily Arctic sea-ice extent minimum was the second-lowest in the 40-year satellite record . <p> The Arctic Ocean is predicted to drop below one million square kilometer --which is an area considered to be ice-free-- in summers before the year 2050 . This will have a significant impact on the environment , influencing ocean circulation and hastening the warming of the Arctic . <p> The sea ice declines , in turn , will trigger the areas of open water to absorb more heat , leading to the increase of ocean temperatures , and this will begin a cycle of warming and melting . <p> According to Professor Dirk Notz from the University of Hamburg , Germany " cutting greenhouse gas emissions remains vital to prevent the worst impacts on the Arctic . However , Professor Notz says that even " if we reduce emissions substantially , keeping global warming levels below 2 ? C , Arctic sea ice will nevertheless disappear occasionally in summers before 2050 . " <h> Future without snow : A next level global warming <p> It is hard to imagine a future without snow , without any chance to ski anymore . Yet , this scenario that today could be part of a science fiction movie , could be the reality of the planet in a distant future . <p> Through a video project ( above ) , MAZCOR Media shows a thought-provoking perspective of a next level global warming . As sad as it may sound , there is now enough evidence proving that climate change could cause the human civilization to collapse by 2050 . <p> We use cookies to ensure you get the best experience on our website . @@61899145 <p> If the world is to meet the Paris Agreement and all energy-related sustainable development goals , roughly 2,000 carbon capture and storage ( CCS ) facilities need to be operating by 2040 , delivering 7% of cumulative emissions reductions . <p> That 's according to the International Energy Agency ( IEA ) who puts the price of a scenario without CCS at more than double the cost . <p> The CCS process involves three major steps : capturing CO2 at the source , compressing it for transportation and then injecting it deep into a rock formation at a carefully selected and safe site , where it is permanently stored . <p> But despite its global recognition as a vital technology in the climate change battle , market uptake for CCS has been slow : there are only 51 large-scale CCS facilities globally -- 19 in operation , four under construction and 28 in various stages of development . <p> " CCS technology comes with a price tag and some solvents currently on the market are not particularly environmentally friendly , " explained Tom White , CEO of CO2 removal specialist C-Capture . <p> This is where C-Capture fits into the CCS picture : the UK company has developed a unique , solvent-based technology which can be deployed on most industrial processes requiring CO2 separation from other gases , including power stations , industrial plants , hydrogen production facilities and bio or natural gas upgrading plants . <p> The technology uses a new class of capture solvents that are not classified as hazardous , are inexpensive and can be manufactured on a large scale from biological sources . <p> " C-Capture 's technology offers many advantages , including reduced emissions , low environmental impact , low corrosivity , but ultimately it offers significant savings in both capital and operational expenditure . This should reduce the barriers to deployment , " White told gasworld . <p> " Supporting infrastructure for CO2 transport and storage is not yet in place , though a lot of hard work is going on to develop projects , business models and roadmaps around the model of industrial clusters in the UK , where shared T&amp;S infrastructure will be implemented . <p> " The recent UK Government commitment of ? 800m to get at least two industrial clusters operational by 2040 demonstrates the commitment and enthusiasm behind decarbonisation of our industrial areas . <p> " Clearly a CO2 utilisation technology at a matching scale that results in a solid product would be a game changer . " <p> Here in an exclusive interview , White ( pictured below , centre ) talks in detail about C-Capture 's gamechanging technology , the company 's involvement in Europe 's first bioenergy carbon capture and storage ( BECCS ) pilot and what support is needed to accelerate commercial deployment of CCS . <p> Source : C-Capture <p> Tom , thanks for your time . For any of our readers who may be unfamiliar with C-Capture , could you tell us a little about the company ? <p> C-Capture was founded in 2009 as a spin-out company from the School of Chemistry at the University of Leeds . <p> It was established with support from IP Group to develop work from Prof. Chis Rayner 's research group at Leeds , where they had been building upon his nearly 20 years ' experience working with CO2 to find new solutions to the carbon capture problem . <p> In late 2011 , we appointed experienced chemist Douglas Barnes and process engineer Caspar Schoolderman who worked together to develop our first-generation technology up to pre-pilot scale . <p> Independent validation of the technology demonstrated it to be as good the then state-of-the-art in terms of energy penalty . This close collaboration between chemists and engineers has been a defining strength and feature of the company from the very beginning . <p> IP Group is a shareholder in our company , alongside BP Ventures and Drax Group . We have also received grant support from the UK Government to support the development and commercialisation of our technology . <p> Let 's talk about C-Capture 's technology . Where did the idea for it come from ? <p> Our initial research was focussed on a combination of an amine and non-amine component and provided both a benchmark for future developments and the experience to bring new ideas to fruition . However , we were also aware that many of the limitations of existing amine-based technologies , including our own , were inherent to all such systems . <p> We knew we needed something completely different for a truly next generation of technology . It was whilst exploring some intuitions during one of our so-called ' Friday afternoon experiments ' that Douglas Barnes , who is now our Head of Chemistry , discovered the basis of our unique solvent chemistry . We quickly realised it was something incredibly special . <p> The experience we 'd gained and the suite of equipment we had put together developing the first solvent allowed us to rapidly optimise the new solvent concept and demonstrate it up to pre-pilot scale . <p> Could you simply explain how the technology works ? <p> C-Capture 's new proprietary solvent captures CO2 from an industrial waste gas by ' washing ' it in an absorber column . The solvent is then heated in a stripper column to release the captured CO2 gas for compression and export , before being recycled to the absorber column again . <p> Our process offers a safer and less expensive alternative to current technologies based on the use of amines . It provides a means to make the removal of CO2 significantly more economical from a range of large-scale processes , such as power generation from coal , gas and biomass , and the production of cement , steel , and aluminium . <p> " These differences are significant enough for C-Capture 's groundbreaking technology to be considered disruptive and is particularly attractive to both end-users and investors ... " <p> How is C-Capture 's technology different to others on the market ? <p> C-Capture 's technology has been specifically developed as an alternative to amine-based systems , which are the main commercial offerings at present . <p> We believe our technology is sufficiently differentiated that it will provide customers with an attractive alternative , with reduced CAPEX , OPEX and environmental risks due to the fundamentally different nature of the technology . <p> What role will it play in tackling climate change ? <p> The fundamentally different chemical processes operating in our process means it represents a true step change in performance , requiring between 1.5-2 GJ/tonne CO2 captured , compared to &gt;2.5 GJ/tonne CO2 for the best of the amine-based systems . <p> These differences are significant enough for C-Capture 's groundbreaking technology to be considered disruptive and is particularly attractive to both end-users and investors . Given sufficient support in funding to enable scale up , C-Capture 's technology has the potential to become the dominant technology with reduced cost and reduced environmental impact and will enable the CCS market to expand more rapidly . <p> What support is needed for the CCS industry as a whole to accelerate commercial deployment ? <p> Certainty of when a viable large industrial scale ( e.g. 10,000 tonnes per day ) CO2 transport and storage infrastructure will be in place . <p> How is C-Capture involved with the BECCS pilot project at Drax 's power plant ? How are things progressing ? <p> C-Capture has had a pilot plant installed within Drax Group 's CCUS Incubation Area at Drax Power Station , North Yorkshire , UK since February 2019 , and currently leads a collaborative project funded by the UK Government 's Department of Business , Energy and Industrial Strategy , to scale up its technology . <p> Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage ( BECCS ) has the potential to generate negative emissions electricity . This approach will be crucial to reach net zero targets . <p> When scaled up , bioenergy with carbon capture and storage technology at Drax could capture up to 16 million tonnes CO2 a year . This would make a huge contribution to the UK 's goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 . <p> We have recently installed an enhanced experimental absorber which tests a new concept and allows more flexibility and accessibility in the system . This important experimental rig -- Europe 's first BECCS pilot -- continues to help us to understand how to optimise our technology at the commercial scale . <p> C-Capture is proud of the potential its technology offers to mitigate climate change as part of the growing market for environmentally conscious power generation and industrial processes . With ongoing support , we will be able to deploy this technology across multiple industries and help deliver the carbon emissions cuts so desperately required . <p> What are the next steps for this project ? <p> As with all engineering projects at this scale , a pre-FEED and FEED study must be carried out , before any engineering design and construction takes place . <p> Drax aims to be using CCS Technology on two of its four biomass generating units by 2030 . <p> We are currently at the very exciting stage of exploring commercial opportunities in other market areas . The markets in which carbon capture technology can be deployed include waste-to-energy or fuel , biogas upgrading , natural gas sweetening , cement , steel , glass manufacture , hydrogen production . We are currently interested in deploying our technology in one or more of these markets , working with the right industry partners . <p> What else does C-Capture have planned for the near future ? <p> Scaling up the technology from 1 tpd to 10,000 tpd at Drax <p> An intermediate project at 100 tpd <p> Internal funding round this year , external funding round next year . <p> Working with industry partners to explore funding opportunities for projects and utilisation options <p> Demonstrating solvent compatibility with flue gases from different industrial sources <p> Expanding the team <p> Worldwide presence <h> Topics <h> Related Articles <p> The World Biogas eFestival , organised last week by the World Biogas Association ( WBA ) to maintain the international dialogue amid global Covid-19 lockdowns , proved to be a great success with more than 300 participants joining the four-day online event from 48 countries around the world . <h> No comments yet <h> Only registered users can comment on this article . <h> About gasworld <p> Month on month , the gasworld website is the market-leading news portal for the global industrial gas sector , growing at an unprecedented rate and keeping its readers at the forefront of breaking news , insightful analysis and must-see features across the industry . Number 8860726 . <p> With the launch of SustainableShips.com and a livestream interview series , ' The Future of Cruising , ' Landry &amp; Kling aims to be an influencer in ' greening ' the cruise industry . <p> Having promoted cruising for more than 38 years , Landry &amp; Kling co-founder/CEO Joyce Landry often felt that her private role as environmentalist , animal activist and advocate to address climate change were in conflict with her cruise industry support . She now seeks to align the company 's culture with her personal values . <h> Mission statement <p> Landry &amp; Kling created SustainableShips.com to help planners , group organizers and consumers evaluate who they want to do business with based on each cruise line 's sustainability practices , to help suppliers of environmental services access the cruise industry and to aid and support the industry toward a more sustainable future . <p> Landry envisions a forum to support and promote lines that are at the forefront of the sustainability movement with proven policies and significant investment in technologies that seek to improve ocean health and provide a healthy environment for passengers and crew . <h> Sustainability assessment <p> The platform will communicate sustainable practices of individual lines to the public , so they can make buying decisions based on their values . It also will provide a sustainability assessment for each line/ship highlighting corporate culture , fuel efficiency , waste handling , plastic reduction/recycling , healthy cleaning products , disinfecting measures and other criteria . This will involve an advisory panel including industry experts and ocean scientists . <h> Marketplace for vendors of sustainable products <p> SustainableShips.com also plans to be a marketplace for vendors of sustainable products and resources aimed at the cruise industry . A further objective includes being a funding source for organizations devoted to ocean cleanup and sustainability . <p> Given L&amp;K 's expertise in meetings at sea , the Miami-based company also aspires to be the mouthpiece for sustainable cruise practices to the corporate MICE market , adhering to policies outlined by the Green Meeting Industry Council . <p> Ultimately , SustainableShips.com wants to be a catalyst for change that inspires cruise lines to do more in the area of sustainability for the greater good . <h> The tipping point <p> ' I 've been working on a sustainability platform for over a year , but it was COVID-19 that gave me the breathing room to bring it to fruition and the team to make it happen , ' Landry said . ' We 're not selling cruises right now , so we were able to put our energy to other uses . ' <p> What pushed Landry over the edge was attending a climate conference at the University of Miami in January and being labeled as the ' enemy ' by one of the attendees who saw her business affiliation . <p> ' That 's when I decided that we -- the cruise industry -- needed to change the narrative , ' Landry said . <p> She thinks cruise lines have a tough time with credibility when it comes to promoting their sustainable practices because that is seen as self-serving . A third party like L&amp;K , she said , can more effectively take this on . <p> Landry cited a growing market of consumers with ' eco-anxiety , ' who are making buying decisions based on sustainability . There is no body or regulatory agency that is qualifying sustainability for the cruise industry , she continued , thus there could be a good amount of ' green washing ' in sustainability statements . <p> ' Our sustainability assessment is a step toward distinguishing the practices and commitment of each cruise line toward sustainability , ' Landry argued . 
@@61899341 <h> Almost ? 10,000 paid for 16 councillors for Monaghan seminar <p> ALMOST ? 10,000 was paid to 16 Clare County Councillors to attend a two-day training seminar in Monaghan last September , new figures have revealed . <p> The Association of Irish Local Government held its Autumn Seminar in The Hillgrove Leisure and Spa Hotel , Monaghan on Wednesday , September 11 and Thursday , September 12 . <p> Councillors were addressed by a number of speakers on Wednesday evening before the re-launch of the updated AILG Brexit Issues Paper that was followed by a hot buffet dinner . <p> Topics such as climate change -- the Role of Local Government , " Met Eireann -- Forecasting Services and Local Authorities " , " The Planning Process and the Office of the Planning Regulator " , as well as a panel discussion between newly-elected councillors with AILG director , Liam Kenny and Local Authority Budgets 2020 were dealt with on Thursday . <p> Councillors who attend the seminar were paid varying amount from ? 329 to ? 743 , which included a seminar fee of ? 140 . <p> While People Before Profit General Election candidate , Theresa O'Donohue supports the provision of training for county councillors , she said this expenditure " sounds exorbitant " . <p> She wondered how much training could be provided in-house at New Road , Ennis for ? 10,000 . <p> Councillor Clare Colleran-Molloy said the AILG is one of the main local authority bodies that hosts biennial seminars where best practice and training can be shared with councillors from all over the country . <p> The Ennis Councillor said this was an important conference for councillors to attend because of the national prominence of this organisation and pointed out there is an advantage to face-to-face training for the participants . <p> Councillor Colleran-Molloy expects that a lot more training will be provided remotely in the future as a result of what has been happening during the Covid-19 pandemic . <p> Councillors Gerry Flynn , Johnny Flynn , Mark Nestor , Ian Lynch and Joe Garrihy and the late Mike McKee received no payments for attending training or conferences while Shane Talty and Joe Killeen did n't claim any expenses for conferences . <h> Classifieds &amp; Acknowledgements <h> In this week 's paper <h> Buy your Digital Edition <h> Photo Sales <h> Advertisement <h> Advertisement <h> @clarechampion <h> Advertisement <h> Advertisement <p> The Clare Champion uses cookies to ensure that we give you the best experience on our website .
